explanation:
### The whole module

```systemverilog
logic [WIDTH-1:0] store [0:DEPTH-1];

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    rdata <= store[raddr];
    if (we) store[waddr] <= wdata;
end
```

### Why the read is registered

Because this is what a block RAM is. On an FPGA, `store` becomes a hard
memory block, and those blocks have a register on the output — the address
goes in on one edge and the data comes out after it. A combinational read
(`assign rdata = store[raddr];`) describes something else: distributed RAM
built out of logic cells, which exists, is much smaller, and is not what you
want for anything deep.

So the one-cycle latency is not an inconvenience the exercise invented. It is
the shape of the thing, and the FIFO in milestone 2 is built around it.

### Why both statements are `<=`

This is the part worth taking away.

A non-blocking assignment has two halves: the right-hand side is *evaluated*
when the statement runs, and the left-hand side is *updated* at the end of the
time step. Every non-blocking assignment in that step evaluates before any of
them updates. So on an edge where `raddr == waddr` and `we` is high:

- `store[raddr]` is read — the old word,
- `wdata` is noted for `store[waddr]`,
- and only then are `rdata` and `store[waddr]` both written.

The old word comes out. That is read-before-write, and it falls out of the
semantics rather than being arranged.

Write either line with `=` and the two statements stop being simultaneous.
`store[waddr] = wdata;` followed by `rdata <= store[raddr];` reads the *new*
word; the other order reads the old one. The behaviour now depends on the
order you happened to type them in, which is the whole reason the rule
"non-blocking in clocked blocks" exists.

### Other ways to write it

Any implementation meeting the specification passes:

- `always @(posedge clk)` instead of `always_ff` — the same thing, with less
  checking from the tools.
- Two separate `always_ff` blocks, one per port. They are still in the same
  time step, so the collision rule is unchanged.
- An explicit `reg [WIDTH-1:0] store [DEPTH-1:0];` with the range the other
  way round. The addresses mean the same thing either way.
